name: Outlook OST/PST Files
location: Classic Outlook cached-mode OST: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Outlook\ (default since Outlook 2013/2016). PST: %USERPROFILE%\Documents\Outlook Files\ (Outlook 2013+ default) or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Outlook\ (legacy/upgraded profiles, hidden folder). Exact per-store paths are recorded in HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\<version>\Outlook\Profiles\<profile>\9375CFF0413111d3B88A00104B2A6676\<service>\001f6700 (or similarly-named binary values) and in the legacy HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows Messaging Subsystem\Profiles\<profile> key. Note: the current "New Outlook" / Outlook for Windows (Monarch) client does not use the classic Cached Exchange Mode/OST model for Exchange/M365 mailboxes - Microsoft does not document an equivalent user-accessible cache file path for it, so do not assume a New-Outlook mailbox has a parseable local OST.
purpose: OST (Offline Storage Table) is a local, encrypted cache of an Exchange/IMAP mailbox used for offline access and cached mode sync; PST (Personal Storage Table) is a self-contained archive/local-delivery store an analyst can open independently of any server. Both are structured containers (folders, messages, contacts, calendar) and are frequently the single richest local source of a user's email history, including items the user believes were deleted from the server.
key_fields: File header 'magic' bytes: PST files begin with the ASCII signature '!BDN'; both formats follow the Microsoft [MS-PST] structured-storage layout (B-tree-on-heap, node database) even though OST is not itself covered by a public Microsoft spec

PST content type flag distinguishes ANSI (pre-Outlook 2003, 2 GB practical size limit) from Unicode (Outlook 2003+, much larger limit) format variants, which affects which parsing tool/library version is required

Per-message MAPI properties, e.g. PR_SUBJECT, PR_SENDER_EMAIL_ADDRESS, PR_MESSAGE_DELIVERY_TIME, PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS (0x007D) - the raw internet header block including the Received chain, preserved even when the item is viewed only through Outlook's rendered UI
Folder hierarchy and per-folder message counts, including Deleted Items and Recoverable Items/Dumpster-equivalent folders inside the store itself

OST encryption cookie tying the file to the specific mailbox/profile that created it (a 'compressible encryption' or 'high encryption' substitution cipher per [MS-PST]), which is why an orphaned OST cannot be opened by Outlook without its originating profile
Attachment objects stored as embedded MAPI attachment streams, extractable independent of whether the parent message is still 'live' in the active view
normal_baseline: A single OST per configured Exchange/IMAP account under the current user's profile, actively growing/syncing, paired with a matching Outlook profile in the registry; any PSTs present correspond to user-created archives or explicitly imported/exported data files the user can account for.
anomalies: An orphaned OST (no matching Outlook profile in the registry, or the referencing profile was recently deleted) - for forensic purposes this is often more valuable than a live one, since it is a frozen snapshot of mailbox state as of the last sync, including server-side items the user has since deleted

A PST located outside the standard Documents\Outlook Files or AppData paths, especially on a removable drive, in a temp/download folder, or with a name suggesting exfiltration staging (e.g., generic or misleading filenames) rather than a normal archive name
PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS present on a message but showing a Received chain inconsistent with the claimed sender domain, or missing entirely on a message type that should carry one
A PST/OST file with a modification time far newer than any Outlook process activity on the host, suggesting the file was copied in from elsewhere rather than generated locally

Registry profile entries (Windows Messaging Subsystem\Profiles or Outlook\Profiles) referencing a PST/OST path that no longer exists on disk - indicates deletion or relocation of a data file after the profile was configured

PST file password-protection (CRC32-based, not strong encryption per historical Outlook implementations) present on a file otherwise inconsistent with the user's normal workflow, suggesting deliberate access restriction
parsing_tools: libpff / pffexport (libyal, open-source, implements the OST/PST structured-storage format)
MFCMAPI (Microsoft, open-source on GitHub - low-level MAPI property browser, can convert between MSG/EML and inspect PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS)
Kernel/Aid4Mail-class commercial e-discovery viewers for bulk PST/OST processing
anti_forensic_notes: OST files cannot be opened outside their originating Outlook profile because the encryption cookie is bound to the mailbox's unique ID validated against the profile/server - this is a legitimate access control, not tampering, but it means an examiner must either restore the original profile context or use a format-aware parser (libpff) that bypasses the MAPI layer entirely. Deleting a PST/OST removes the local copy, but for an OST this is low-impact anti-forensics since the data still exists server-side and Outlook will simply resync; deleting a PST used for local-only archiving or POP3 delivery is high-impact since no server copy exists. Registry profile remnants (Windows Messaging Subsystem\Profiles, Outlook\Profiles) can survive deletion of the data file itself and are useful for proving a store once existed at a specific path.
